problem: Open-source LLM/MLLM navigators for zero-shot VLN-CE (e.g. Open-Nav) lag far behind closed-source GPT-based ones. The paper attributes this to 'navigation amnesia': textualized observations lose discriminative visual cues and cause loops, and small context windows lead to drift from the instruction over long horizons.
motivation: Closed-source models bring API cost, latency and privacy risks from uploading visual streams, so on-robot open-source models matter for home and industrial deployment. Drawing on Hippocampal Memory Indexing Theory, the authors separate short-term visual memory (state localization) from long-term semantic memory (global goal).
key_idea: Add a hierarchical memory system to an open-source MLLM navigator: a short-term visual-graph Localer that detects revisits and softly constrains exploration, and a long-term Globaler that keeps a global instruction schema and origin direction.
insight: Both memory modules are training-free prompt-level injections that fix distinct failure modes (looping vs. drift). The component ablation (figure only) shows that removing either the Localer or the Globaler degrades performance and that combining both is best. Larger MLLMs make better navigators (Qwen2-VL-72B > InternVL-3.5-8B > LLaVA-OV-1.5-8B > Qwen2.5-VL-7B).
method: Waypoint predictor and perception: an OpenNav-style transformer predicts K=5 candidate waypoints from 12-view RGB-D; RAM and SpatialBot turn each candidate view into textual object and spatial descriptions.
Visual Graph Memory: nodes store a CLIP embedding (512-d), last-visit step and visit count; the current location embedding is a forward-biased weighted aggregation of multi-view CLIP features.

Localization and graph update: cosine matching against nodes, revisit if similarity >= adaptive threshold (init 0.85, relaxed as the graph grows), otherwise a new node; momentum update alpha=0.15; edges link consecutive nodes.

Short-term memory injection: per-direction novelty is computed as one minus the max similarity to the graph; high-visit, low-novelty directions are deprioritized via soft constraints and summarized as text in the prompt.
Globaler global extraction: one MLLM call extracts a schema {PrimaryDir, FinalTarget, NavPattern} from the instruction, cached as long-term memory.

Origin tracking and injection: a CameFrom variable (opposite of the last move), plus a summary of the last k=5 actions; a prompt asks the MLLM to check that the current direction aligns with the global schema.
Closed loop: the MLLM navigator does subgoal decomposition, progress estimation and waypoint selection; a low-level planner executes it.

setting.backbone: Qwen2-VL-72B (frozen, 4-bit quantized in deployment; the text also names Qwen2-72B-Instruct) plus CLIP encoder, RAM, SpatialBot and a pretrained waypoint predictor
setting.training_data: none (training-free); waypoint predictor pretrained as in Open-Nav
setting.action_space: predicted waypoints (K=5) executed via low-level MOVE FORWARD 0.25 m / TURN 30° / STOP
setting.simulator: Habitat (R2R-CE, MP3D) plus a real Unitree Go2W robot

numbers.eval_set_note: 100 episodes under the Open-Nav / SmartWay evaluation frameworks

numbers_note: The ablation is only shown as a figure, with no numbers in the text. The real-world backbone is assumed to be the main model, which the text does not state explicitly.
results: On R2R-CE, HiMemVLN-Qwen2-VL-72B reaches SR 30, SPL 26.85 and OSR 36, versus Open-Nav-Llama3.1 at SR 16 and Open-Nav-Qwen2-72B at SR 14. It roughly matches SmartWay (SR 29) and beats Open-Nav-GPT4 (SR 19). In the real world SR is 32 versus 18 for Open-Nav.
limitations: Evaluation is small: 100 simulated episodes and 20 real-world instructions, with no full val-unseen results.
Absolute SR (~30%) is still far below supervised methods (48–60%); the method depends on the waypoint predictor and textualized perception.
Component ablation is figure-only and there are no hyperparameter or latency analyses.
